question: Which of the following statements regarding 친자관계 is incorrect? (다툼이 있는 경우, 판례에 의함)
A: 당사자 사이에 친생자관계가 없음을 확인한다는 내용이 포함되어 있는 조정이나 재판상 화해가 성립하더라도 it has no effect.
B: ｢민법｣ 제777조에서 정한 친족이라도 ｢민법｣ 제865조에서 정한 이해관계인에 해당하는 경우에만 친생자관계존부확인의 소의 원고적격이 인정된다.
C: 피상속인 甲(女)의 공동상속인 乙과 丙이 이미 상속재산을 분할 또는 처분한 이후에 丁이 甲의 자(子)임이 친생자관계 존재확인판결의 확정으로 명백히 밝혀진 경우, 인지의 소급효 제한에 관한 ｢민법｣ 제860조 단서는 적용되지 아니하므로 丁 cannot deny the validity of the division or disposition made by 乙과 丙.
D: 정상적으로 혼인생활을 하고 있는 부부 사이에서 인공수정 자녀가 출생하는 경우 the child born through artificial insemination is presumed to be the husband’s child, and 남편이 인공수정에 동의하였다가 나중에 이를 번복하고 친생부인의 소를 제기하는 것은 허용되지 않는다.
E: 성전환자의 기본권 보호와 미성년 자녀의 보호 및 복리와의 조화를 이룰 수 있도록 법익의 균형을 위한 여러 사정들을 고려하여 실질적으로 판단하지 아니한 채 단지 성전환자에게 미성년 자녀가 있다는 사정만을 이유로 성별 정정을 불허하여서는 아니 된다.

{"[2015MEU0000]": "We 판단한다 the grounds for appeal.
1. Summary of the case and issues
가. Summary of the case
Non-party 1(사망 on 1909. 8. 10.) was designated on 2010. 8. 15. as a recipient candidate for the Patriotic Medal, Grade 4. After Non-party 3, who is a child of Non-party 1’s eldest daughter Non-party 2(사망), was 인정된 through 행정소송 as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence(the version before amendment by Act No. 11332 on 2012. 2. 17.; hereinafter the “former Independence Merit Treatment Act”), the Plaintiff, who is the grandson of Non-party 1’s eldest son Non-party 4(사망), filed this action against the Prosecutor seeking, among other things, a 확인 that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2.
The lower court dismissed this action as inadmissible because even if the Plaintiff obtained a judgment confirming the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship as above, he could not be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, and there was no other legal interest in seeking that confirmation. In response, the Plaintiff appealed, arguing that because he is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1 within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, he necessarily has an interest in filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, in line with prior Supreme Court precedents.

나. Issue in this case
The issue is whether the Plaintiff, merely because he is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1, may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. To decide this issue, we first examine the scope of standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Civil Act Article 865, and then consider whether the prior Supreme Court precedents holding that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file such an action merely on the basis of such status relationship should be maintained.

2. Standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Civil Act Article 865
가. Persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship
A parent-child relationship, as 친자관계, is divided into a natural parent-child relationship based on blood ties and an adoptive parent-child relationship based on the parties’ intent. Regarding the natural parent-child relationship, the Civil Act provides several provisions for determining the existence or dissolution of the relationship, unlike the mother-child relationship, which is clearly determined by the natural facts of conception and birth. These include the provision on the presumption of legitimacy that a child conceived during marriage is presumed to be the child of the husband(Article 844 paragraph (1)); the provisions on an action for disavowal of paternity, which is the method for rebutting that presumption(Articles 846 through 851); the provisions on the court’s determination of paternity where a remarried woman gives birth(Article 845); the provisions on acknowledgment of a child born out of wedlock(Article 855 paragraph (1) and Article 863); and the provisions on revocation of acknowledgment and an action to object to acknowledgment(Articles 861 and 862). Accordingly, in litigation seeking establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it is in principle the person entitled to file the action expressly specified in each of the above provisions who may sue after satisfying the requirements prescribed by those provisions.
Civil Act Article 865 paragraph (1)(hereinafter the “provision at issue”) provides: “A person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions of Article 845, Article 846, Article 848, Article 850, Article 851, Article 862, or Article 863 may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground.” This is intended to allow filing of an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship so as to correct a mismatch between the legal parent-child relationship and the parent-child relationship stated in the family relations register.
Considering that the provision at issue does not directly and concretely specify who may file such an action, but instead cites provisions concerning other litigation procedures with similar purposes and grants standing as Plaintiff to the person entitled to file each such action while only changing the grounds, the action under the provision at issue is supplementary to other litigation procedures concerning the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship.
In light of the form, wording, and structure of the provision at issue, the characteristics of the litigation procedures prescribed by the above provisions, and the supplementary nature of this action, it is appropriate to view the persons who may file such an action as limited to the persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue.

나. Specific scope of standing as Plaintiff
(1) Father, mother, and child as parties to a natural parent-child relationship
The father, mother, and child, who are the parties to a natural parent-child relationship, are persons who may file an action pursuant to Civil Act Articles 845, 846, 862, and 863, which are listed in the provision at issue, and therefore may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the cause is another ground.

(2) Lineal descendants of the child and their legal representatives
The lineal descendants of the child, who is a party to a natural parent-child relationship, and their legal representatives are persons who may file an action pursuant to Civil Act Article 863, which is listed in the provision at issue, and therefore may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the cause is another ground.

(3) Adult guardians, testamentary executors, and lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife
Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are listed in the provision at issue, are all provisions that supplementarily expand standing as Plaintiff on the premise of Civil Act Article 846, which is the basic provision regarding standing as Plaintiff in an action for disavowal of paternity. Accordingly, adult guardians, testamentary executors, and the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife, who are persons entitled to sue under Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, should be regarded as having standing only when they satisfy the requirements for filing suit under those provisions. In other words, an adult guardian may newly file such an action where the husband or wife has come under adult guardianship(Article 848); a testamentary executor may newly file such an action where the husband or wife has indicated by will an intent to deny the natural parent-child relationship(Article 850); and the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife may newly file such an action where the husband dies before the child’s birth or the husband or wife dies within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity(Article 851). If they do not satisfy the above requirements, it cannot be said that they necessarily have standing as Plaintiff to file an action under those provisions.

(4) Interested persons
An interested person may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground pursuant to Civil Act Article 862, which is listed in the provision at issue. Here, an interested person means a third party who has a legal interest, such as obtaining certain rights or being relieved from obligations, by a final judgment stating that a natural parent-child relationship exists or does not exist between other persons. Accordingly, only where the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between other persons will, by judicial determination, have a concrete impact on the interested person’s own rights or obligations concerning inheritance, support, or the like, or on his or her legal status, may such person file an action as an interested person.
A person who files such an action while asserting that he or she is the natural father or natural mother of a child, even though no kinship relationship is stated in the family relations register, is included among interested persons because, depending on the result of the judgment, that person will be directly affected with respect to the very existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship with the party.
In the end, unless the Plaintiff who filed the action is a person whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized as described in (1), (2), and (3) above, standing exists only where the Plaintiff falls within the category of interested persons referred to here. Whether a person falls within such an interested person category must be determined by individually examining, based on the Plaintiff’s allegations and the circumstances shown in the pleadings, what concrete impact exists on the Plaintiff’s rights or obligations concerning inheritance, support, or the like, or on the Plaintiff’s legal status.

3. Whether kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship
가. Prior Supreme Court precedents
In Supreme Court en banc Decision 80MEU60, rendered on 1981. 10. 13., the Court held that Article 35 of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation(enacted by Act No. 803 on 1961. 12. 6., effective as of 1962. 1. 1., and repealed by Act No. 4300 on 1990. 12. 31.; hereinafter the same) applied mutatis mutandis Article 26, which provides that “the party, the legal representative, or the kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may file an action for nullity of marriage at any time,” to the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Civil Act Article 865, and thus held that standing as Plaintiff was necessarily recognized merely by the fact that one is in a kinship relationship prescribed in Civil Act Article 777.
Thereafter, the Supreme Court reached the same conclusion not only in cases governed by the former Act on Personal Status Litigation(see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 81MEU77 rendered on 1983. 3. 8., and Supreme Court Decision 90MEU347 rendered on 1991. 5. 28.), but also in cases governed by the Family Litigation Act newly enacted upon the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation(enacted by Act No. 4300 on 1990. 12. 31. and effective as of 1991. 1. 1.; hereinafter the same)(see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on 1998. 10. 20., and Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on 2004. 2. 12.).

나. Necessity of changing the precedent
However, in light of the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and other statutes, the enactment and implementation of the Family Litigation Act, changes in the family system such as the abolition of the head-of-family system, the special characteristics of status litigation, the diversification of family composition and respect for the parties’ intent in that regard, and balance with other litigation procedures aimed at the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it must be concluded that the prior Supreme Court precedents holding that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may necessarily be filed merely because one is kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 can no longer be maintained. The detailed reasons are as follows.
(1) The former Act on Personal Status Litigation, which set special provisions regarding litigation procedures concerning personal status in relation to the Civil Procedure Act, contained an express provision(Articles 35 and 26) stating that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file such an action. In fact, this became the core basis of the prior Supreme Court precedents. However, unlike the former Act on Personal Status Litigation, the Family Litigation Act, which integrated the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the former Family Affairs Adjudication Act(enacted by Act No. 1375 on 1963. 7. 31., effective as of 1963. 10. 1., and repealed by Act No. 4300 on 1990. 12. 31.), contains no provision at all concerning who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The Family Litigation Act merely applies mutatis mutandis the provisions concerning the opposing party in an action for nullity of marriage, etc.(Article 24) to an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, while not applying the provision concerning the person entitled to file suit(Article 23). Accordingly, with the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the implementation of the Family Litigation Act, the legal basis of the prior Supreme Court precedents disappeared.
(2) As legal norms surrounding family relations and social circumstances changed, social perceptions regarding natural parent-child relationships, which together with marital relations form the foundation of family relations, also changed.
At the time of the enactment of the Civil Act and even after the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the enactment of the Family Litigation Act, for a considerable period of time Korean civil law maintained the household head system, under which family relations were publicly recorded in the family register organized by household unit based on the head of family. At that time, most persons in a kinship relationship, such as the lineal ascendants and lineal descendants of the head of family, collateral relatives, and their spouses, were entered in the family register as members of the household centered on the head of family. However, with the 2005 amendment to the Civil Act, the household head system was completely abolished and reorganized into a family system centered on spouses and children, and as of 2008. 1. 1., when the Act on the Registration, etc. of Family Relations(enacted by Act No. 8435 on 2007. 5. 17.; hereinafter the “Family Relations Registration Act”) came into force, the family relations registration register replacing the family register has recorded, centered on the individual, the occurrence and changes of family relations through marriage, birth, and the like. In addition, in our society, the nuclear family consisting of parents and unmarried children has already become the norm rather than the traditional extended family, and with the progress of urbanization and industrialization, individualism and liberalism have become widely prevalent in family life as well.
In light of these legal and social changes concerning the family system and the like, unlike the period when the household head system was maintained, the legal and social basis for viewing kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 as having a close status-related legal interest has weakened today.
(3) The action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a litigation procedure designed to correct entries in the family relations registration register that do not correspond to the true blood relationship(Family Relations Registration Act Article 107). However, today family relations are formed not only on the basis of blood relations but also diversely on the basis of the parties’ intent. The Supreme Court has held that the presumption of legitimacy also applies to a child born through artificial insemination during marriage, and that even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by a wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, it cannot be said that the presumption of legitimacy does not apply(see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016MEU2510 rendered on 2019. 10. 23.). The Supreme Court has also held that where a party registers a child as born of the party’s own biological child with the intent to create an adoptive parent-child relationship, the effect of adoption is recognized if the requirements for adoption are satisfied(however, the Civil Act amended by Act No. 11300 on 2012. 2. 10. and effective as of 2013. 7. 1. requires approval from the Family Court as a requirement for adoption of a minor), and that a claim for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted in relation thereto(see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2000MEU1493 rendered on 2001. 5. 24.). This is because legal protection is needed not only where the presumption of legitimacy applies to a parent-child relationship formed without a blood relationship, but also where, even if the presumption of legitimacy does not apply, that parent-child relationship has been substantially formed on the basis of the parties’ intent. Accordingly, while respecting the free intent of the parties regarding the formation of the legal parent-child relationship underlying marriage and family relations, it is necessary to impose certain limitations so that third parties do not improperly intervene in that regard.
(4) An action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship falls under a “Category A family litigation case” under the Family Litigation Act(Article 2 paragraph (1) subparagraph 1(a) of the Family Litigation Act). The effect of a judgment granting such an action extends to third parties as well(Article 21 of the same Act), and the court must investigate facts and take necessary evidence ex officio and may examine the parties at any time(Article 17 of the same Act). In particular, considering the reality that blood relationship can now be proved relatively easily through DNA testing and the like, broadly viewing the scope of third parties who may contest the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship in the name of finding the truth of blood ties and allowing the case to proceed to the merits is highly likely to undermine the stability of status order and infringe the parties’ autonomous decision-making regarding marriage and family life. Accordingly, it is not desirable to expand arbitrarily, by interpretation and without an express statutory basis, the scope of third parties who may bring such an action.
Although the Family Litigation Act provides in Article 24 paragraph (2) and Article 28 for cases in which a third party files an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, these are provisions concerning the opposing party(defendant capacity), not the person entitled to sue, and therefore cannot serve as a basis for expanding the scope of persons entitled to file suit.
(5) Since an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is supplementary to other litigation procedures aimed at the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it is clear that where such an action may be filed under another litigation procedure, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted.
Meanwhile, where there is a dispute concerning a legal natural parent-child relationship, such an action is often used in place of other litigation procedures whose filing requirements are relatively strict, and current practice also shows such a tendency. The Supreme Court has extended the legal principles concerning this action to adoptive parent-child relationships as well(see Supreme Court Decision 92MEU372 rendered on 1993. 7. 16.), and moreover, the filing period is not prescribed except where one or both parties to the natural parent-child relationship have died(Civil Act Article 865 paragraph (2)).
In this way, the filing requirements for this action have already been relaxed in several respects, and further expanding the scope of standing as Plaintiff to kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 is not balanced even when compared with the other litigation procedures described above. This is even more so because of the risk that this action may be distorted into a means of circumventing the requirements or restrictions established by statutory provisions concerning other litigation procedures.
(6) The natural parent-child relationship, which forms the basis of status relationships, does not end merely as a matter between the parties, but may affect inheritance issues among relatives and various other legal relationships based on kinship, such as parental authority and support(see Supreme Court Decision 2004MEU405 rendered on 2004. 6. 24.). It is therefore of course necessary that certain third parties also be given the opportunity to contest the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through a proper judicial procedure. Since the Civil Act, in the provision at issue, allows a third party who is not a party to the natural parent-child relationship to contest its existence or nonexistence if that third party qualifies as an interested person, a third party who is kin also has standing if that person qualifies as an interested person. Accordingly, even if not all kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 are uniformly granted standing as Plaintiff, it cannot be said that the rights or right to a judicial remedy of third parties who have a legal interest in the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship are unjustly restricted.

다. Change in precedent
Accordingly, Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on 1998. 10. 20., which held in relation to cases governed by the Family Litigation Act that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, absent special circumstances, have a litigation interest in filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship merely because of such status relationship, and Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on 2004. 2. 12. and other judgments to the same effect are changed to the extent they are inconsistent with the view of this judgment.

4. Determination in this case
가. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the following facts may be found.
(1) Non-party 1 was designated on 2010. 8. 15. as a recipient candidate for the Patriotic Medal, Grade 4, and Non-party 1’s children were the eldest son Non-party 4, the eldest daughter Non-party 2, and the second daughter Non-party 5. Non-party 4 and his spouse and children, as well as Non-party 5 and her spouse, all died before the date on which the recipient candidate was designated, and the only surviving child of Non-party 5 was Non-party 6(date of birth omitted, male). The Plaintiff is the grandson of Non-party 4.
(2) On 2010. 8. 30., Non-party 6 applied to the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs for registration as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under Article 6 of the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, on the ground that he is a grandson of Non-party 1, and was registered on 2011. 11. 24. as the first-priority bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence.
(3) Meanwhile, Non-party 3(date of birth omitted, female) applied on 2011. 11. 25. to the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs for registration as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, asserting that she is a child of Non-party 1’s eldest daughter Non-party 2 and thus the first in priority among Non-party 1’s grandchildren, but the head of the Gwangju Regional Office rejected the application on 2011. 11. 30. Thereafter, Non-party 3 filed an action for cancellation of the refusal to register her as a person of distinguished service to independence against the head of the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs(Gwangju District Court Case No. 2011GUHAP4510), obtained a judgment in her favor on all claims, and that judgment later became final and conclusive after appeal and further appeal.

나. Examining the above factual relations in light of the legal principles discussed above leads to the following conclusion.
(1) The Plaintiff is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1 as Non-party 1’s lineal descendant(great-grandchild), but he does not fall within the category of persons whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized under the provision at issue.
(2) According to Article 5 paragraph (1) and Article 12 paragraph (2), paragraph (4) subparagraph 1 of the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, compensation is paid only to one first-priority bereaved family member among the person of distinguished service to independence and his or her bereaved family members, and the scope of bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation is limited in the order of spouse, child, grandchild, and daughter-in-law of the person of distinguished service to independence, with the older person receiving priority if there are two or more persons of the same rank. Therefore, under the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, the Plaintiff, who is merely the great-grandchild of Non-party 1, cannot be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, and since Non-party 6 in addition to Non-party 3(child of the eldest daughter Non-party 2) appears to be alive as a grandchild of Non-party 1, the Plaintiff cannot be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence even if he obtains a judgment confirming the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2. Nor does the question whether the Plaintiff may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence depend on whether Non-party 2 is the child of Non-party 7, the wife of Non-party 1.
(3) Even if a judgment confirming that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2, and between Non-party 7 and Non-party 2, respectively, becomes final and conclusive, the Plaintiff cannot be said to have a legal interest therein. Accordingly, this action must be regarded as unlawful because it was filed by a person lacking standing as Plaintiff.

다. The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper as it follows the legal principles discussed above. The lower court did not err, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by misapprehending the law on standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, by failing to conduct the necessary examination, or by exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the principles of logic and experience.

5. Conclusion
The Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. Except for the separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang and Justice Min Yoo-sook, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are supplementary opinions by Justice Park Jeong-hwa, Justice Kim Seon-su, and Justice Roh Jeong-hee regarding the majority opinion.

6. Separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang and Justice Min Yoo-sook
We agree with the majority opinion regarding the change in Supreme Court precedent. However, we differ from the majority opinion as to the scope of persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship and whether the Plaintiff in this case falls within that category.

가. First, our view regarding the change in precedent.
(1) The provision at issue states, “A person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions of Article 845, Article 846, Article 848, Article 850, Article 851, Article 862, or Article 863 may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground.” Accordingly, it is clear from the wording of the provision at issue that the person entitled to file such an action is limited to the persons specified therein.
However, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation provided that “kin under Civil Act Article 777” may file such an action(Articles 26 and 35). Yet, since the provision at issue in the Civil Act had already expressly specified the person entitled to sue with respect to this action, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation’s inclusion of a separate provision concerning the person entitled to sue created systemic confusion. On 1990. 12. 31., the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the former Family Affairs Adjudication Act were both repealed and the integrated Family Litigation Act came into force, and the Family Litigation Act deleted the provision from the former Act on Personal Status Litigation concerning the person entitled to file such an action. With the implementation of the Family Litigation Act, the overlapping provisions were eliminated, and the persons entitled to file such an action became governed solely by the provision at issue in the Civil Act.
(2) Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on 1998. 10. 20., which the majority opinion cites as a precedent to be changed, held that if a person is kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, that person may file such an action merely because of being in such a status relationship, and thus failed properly to reflect the changes brought about by the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the implementation of the Family Litigation Act. However, Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on 2004. 2. 12., also cited as a precedent to be changed, unlike Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585, held that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may file such an action as an “interested person” who is a person entitled to sue under the provision at issue. Accordingly, if one takes the later Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 as the benchmark, the current Supreme Court precedent is not that kin under Civil Act Article 777 “become persons entitled to file such an action even though there is no longer any legal basis”(the premise of the majority opinion), but rather that they “become persons entitled to file such an action as interested persons under the provision at issue.”
(3) Although the Civil Act as amended by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13. reduced the scope of kin, Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503, which held that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 necessarily fall within the category of “interested persons,” may still be evaluated as merely following the repealed provisions of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation, and it is therefore appropriate to change it. Accordingly, the change in precedent should target the holding that “kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 fall within the category of interested persons under the provision at issue merely because of their status relationship,” and we agree with the majority opinion as to such change.

나. In this case, the issue is whether the Plaintiff, as the great-grandchild of Non-party 1, falls within the persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue, namely “lineal descendants of the husband or wife” or “interested persons.” Since we differ from the majority opinion on this point, we set forth our view in detail below.
(1) Before addressing the issue, we first consider the majority opinion concerning the necessity of changing precedent.
(a) According to the majority opinion, because family relations today are formed diversely not only on the basis of blood relations but also on the basis of the parties’ intent, the free intent of the parties should also be respected as to the existence or nonexistence of a legal natural parent-child relationship. However, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a judicial procedure for confirming the existence or nonexistence of a true blood relationship, and the existence or nonexistence of the legal natural parent-child relationship that is the subject matter of the litigation is not of a nature that can be determined by the free intent of the parties.
Under the Civil Act, the chapter on kin(Part IV) is broadly structured around Chapter 3, “Marriage,” and Chapter 4, “Parents and Child,” and Chapter 4, “Parents and Child,” is again divided into provisions concerning Section 1, “Natural Child,” and Section 2, “Adopted Child.” This shows that the relationship between parents and children is formed on the basis of blood ties and the parties’ intent, but that among them the natural parent-child relationship is based on blood ties(the Supreme Court en banc Decision 2000MEU1493 rendered on 2001. 5. 24., cited by the majority opinion, concerns the legal doctrine of adoption, under which the parent-child relationship is formed by the parties’ intent).
In addition, in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, admission of the claim and confession are not permitted(Article 12 of the Family Litigation Act), and the prior mediation principle also does not apply(Article 50 paragraph (1) of the same Act), so it is impossible in such proceedings to determine the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by the parties’ intent. Disposition by the parties’ free will concerning the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted.
(b) The majority opinion takes the view that the scope of persons entitled to sue should be limited so that third parties do not improperly intervene in family relations. We fully agree that private life and domestic peace should be protected against threats by third parties. Indeed, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016MEU2510 rendered on 2019. 10. 23. held, in substance, that in a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy applies, third parties must be prevented from intervening indirectly in another person’s family matters by allowing only an action for disavowal of paternity, which strictly limits the persons entitled to sue and the filing period.
However, the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship in this case is fundamentally different from an action for disavowal of paternity in this respect. Because a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy applies can be denied only by a judgment in an action for disavowal of paternity, there is practical benefit in limiting the persons entitled to sue in order to achieve that purpose. By contrast, a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy does not apply may not only be contested through such an action, but when it becomes a preliminary issue in other litigation procedures such as civil litigation, anyone may allege and prove its nonexistence in that litigation procedure(see Supreme Court Decision 78DA71 rendered on 1978. 4. 11.). Therefore, even if the scope of third parties who may file such an action is limited, such limitation cannot prevent them from contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through civil litigation, etc. Limiting the scope of persons entitled to file such an action, as in the majority opinion, has little practical effect in preventing third parties from intervening in another person’s family matters and cannot be said to be an appropriate method. Rather, permitting certain third parties to file such an action makes it possible to finally resolve disputes surrounding status relationships and thereby also ensure the accuracy and authenticity of the family relations registration register. This is because only when the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is determined in the “disposition” of a judgment by filing such an action can the family relations registration register be corrected, the effect of a judgment granting the claim extends to third parties as well, and special provisions such as orders to undergo testing are more helpful in ascertaining the true blood relationship.
Even in this case, Non-party 3, a relative whose interests are opposed to those of the Plaintiff, had already, through 행정소송, asserted that there is a natural parent-child relationship between her mother and Non-party 1, obtained a final and conclusive judgment in her favor, and the reasons for that judgment include a determination regarding blood relationship. It does not appear easy to preserve the peace of these families merely by blocking the Plaintiff’s filing of this subsequent action.
(c) Looking at the statistics on “litigation relating to parent-child relationships” in the Judicial Yearbook published annually by the courts over the past five years, actions for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship account for 75 to 80 percent of all litigation relating to parent-child relationships, occupying an overwhelming share. In such actions, the rate at which the Plaintiff’s claim is granted at first instance exceeds 75 percent, and the appeal rate is only around 1 percent. Unlike the fact that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is prescribed under the Civil Act as a supplementary form of litigation, in practice it has become the principal form of litigation relating to parent-child relationships, and although the Family Litigation Act is structured to have an adversarial-party framework, in practice there are mostly not serious disputes between the relevant parties concerning the very “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship.”
Even today, as in the past when public registers, etc. for publicizing status relationships were not adequately established, birth registrations and the like are often made contrary to the actual blood relationship due to legal restrictions or personal circumstances. Under the Supreme Court precedents that a family relations registration register cannot be corrected absent a final and conclusive judgment concerning matters that have a significant impact under the law of kinship or inheritance, as prescribed in Article 2 paragraphs (1) and (2) of the Family Litigation Act(see the Supreme Court en banc Decision on correction of family registers, 93SEU14, 15, 16 rendered on 1993. 5. 22.), even if there is no substantive dispute between the parties regarding the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, which is a family litigation with an adversarial structure, must nonetheless be filed in order to correct the family relations registration register(see the above statistics on the rate at which claims are granted and the appeal rate).
Furthermore, whether a person falls within the category of persons entitled to file such an action is a matter of standing as Plaintiff, which is a litigation requirement, and thus a matter to be examined ex officio. The more strictly the scope of standing as Plaintiff is limited or the more complex the criteria for judgment are set, the more likely it is, as noted above, that even where there is no substantive dispute between the parties regarding the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship, the court will ex officio examine standing as Plaintiff and dismiss the action, resulting in an increased number of such cases.
(d) The majority opinion is concerned that if the scope of persons entitled to sue is broadened, such an action may be distorted into a means of evading legal restrictions. However, that is a matter for the family court handling the case to faithfully examine the relevant issues and distinguish the genuine from the spurious; it is not a matter to be resolved by limiting standing as Plaintiff and thereby blocking the filing of the action itself.
(2) We now consider the first issue, namely the part of the majority opinion that limited the filing requirements for “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife.”
(a) The majority opinion states that “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” may file such an action only where the husband dies before the child’s birth or the husband or wife dies within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity.
However, because such an action is a litigation procedure entirely different from an action for disavowal of paternity in terms of litigation structure and legal nature, it is not appropriate to require separate conditions, as in an action for disavowal of paternity, even when lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife file such an action.
(b) An action for disavowal of paternity may be filed only by one of the spouses, and therefore it is necessary to make provision for the case where the person entitled to file it has died. Civil Act Article 851 provides that in such a case, the “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants” of the husband or wife may file the action. However, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship expressly contemplates, from the outset, filing not only by the parties to the natural parent-child relationship but also by third parties(Article 24 paragraph (2) and Article 28 of the Family Litigation Act). Therefore, the structure in which, if the party entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity dies, his or her lineal ascendants or lineal descendants become supplementary persons entitled to sue does not fit such an action.
An example will clarify this. Since the mother-child relationship arises from the natural facts of conception and birth, the wife(hereinafter “A”) may file such an action against a person recorded in the family relations register as her biological child(hereinafter “B”), alleging the nonexistence of a blood relationship without any time limit, and if A dies, A’s lineal descendants may file such an action against B. In such a case, the majority opinion says that A’s lineal descendants may file such an action only if A died within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity(two years from the date on which the cause for disavowal was known). However, since there is no room for the presumption of legitimacy itself to arise between A and B, it is impossible to assume a date on which the cause for disavowal became known, and the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity cannot run either. According to the majority opinion, it is difficult to tell how one is to determine whether the requirement of the filing-period limitation has been met. Moreover, while A could have filed the action at any time during her lifetime, once A dies, one arrives at the strange conclusion that, retroactively to some specific point in the past, the filing period had already expired.
(c) The parties to a natural parent-child relationship are the parent and the child. The lineal descendants of the child may file such an action pursuant to the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 863 without satisfying any other filing requirements, and the majority opinion does not differ on this point.
If the lineal descendants of the child are allowed to file such an action without any further restriction, it is balanced and natural in terms of textual interpretation to regard the lineal descendants of the parent as likewise being able to file such an action without any time limit. In practice, there is much greater possibility or necessity for the lineal descendants of the parent to file an action contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship after the parent’s death than there is for the lineal descendants of the child to do so after the child’s death.
(d) In addition, where the parent, who is a party to the natural parent-child relationship, dies without filing an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, and only a testamentary executor is appointed, or where adult guardianship has commenced while the parent had not filed such an action, the adult guardian and testamentary executor, as persons entitled to sue, will have the question of whether filing is permitted separately determined under the Civil Act provisions concerning the scope of their duties even if standing as Plaintiff is recognized under the provision at issue, and thus the issue differs from the present case.
(e) The reasons why descendants file an action after the parent has not, during the parent’s lifetime, resolved the family relations registration register so that it matches the blood relationship vary depending on individual circumstances and family relations. There may be cases in which a child files an action against the parent’s wishes during the parent’s lifetime, but as in the Judicial Yearbook statistics mentioned above, in most cases the first-instance judgment in favor of the Plaintiff is accepted by both sides and becomes final and conclusive as rendered. There are even cases where a person who, because there was no blood relationship and thus no substantive status as a child during the parent’s lifetime, claims inheritance rights on the basis of the family relations registration register after the parent’s death, causing other heirs to bring litigation.
(3) We now consider the second issue, namely the part of the majority opinion that explained the requirements for an “interested person.”
(a) The majority opinion states that an “interested person,” as a person entitled to file such an action, is a third party having a legal interest, such as obtaining certain rights or being relieved from obligations, by a final judgment confirming the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between other persons. The majority opinion’s view on this point is almost identical to the holdings in Supreme Court Decision 4293MINSANG314 rendered on 1960. 9. 29. and Supreme Court Decision 90MEU88 rendered on 1990. 7. 13., so it is in effect understood as relying on those decisions. However, because all of those Supreme Court decisions were holdings in cases governed by the already repealed former Act on Personal Status Litigation, it is not appropriate for the majority opinion to continue to rely on them.
(b) The primary criterion for determining the scope of an interested person should be whether the person suffers detriment in his or her legal status based on a status relationship due to the registration of a natural parent-child relationship different from the true blood relationship in the current family relations registration register, and whether there exists a legally protectable interest worth correcting through a judgment confirming the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The criterion presented by the majority opinion, namely whether the person “obtains certain rights or is relieved from obligations,” is not an appropriate criterion because it may extend to cases where there is no effect on status relationships but only a property interest(for example, an insurance beneficiary or a creditor of an heir).
(c) If whether a person qualifies as an interested person is to be determined case by case on the basis of the circumstances shown in the Plaintiff’s allegations or pleadings, there is a risk of a side effect whereby the focus of the family court’s examination and determination shifts from the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” which is the subject matter of the litigation, to the “impact on rights, obligations, or legal status.” This is because, in litigation procedures in which the court must determine the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the Plaintiff’s order of succession or order of support must first be alleged and examined in order to determine standing as Plaintiff.
Such side effects are more pronounced where the legal interest is related to public law status. The “impact on the rights and obligations of third parties” may appear, as in this case, in the form of public-law legal relationships where special statutes, including the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, provide for payment of compensation or benefits to a certain range of “bereaved family members,” etc. In such cases, if the above principle is applied in determining whether a person qualifies as an interested person, the family court will bear the burden of ex officio examining and determining the compensation standards, the beneficiaries of benefits, and the scope of bereaved family members prescribed by various administrative statutes. It cannot be said to be appropriate to compel interpretation and determination of administrative statutes, which are not within the family court’s area of expertise, in a family litigation case.
In fact, before determining the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” which was the cause of action, the lower court in this case examined in detail the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act and whether the Plaintiff could be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence. It is not desirable for such examination and determination of administrative statutes to become the center of an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, which is a family litigation case.

다. In conclusion, we consider this case.
(1) Since the Plaintiff is a lineal descendant of Non-party 1 and Non-party 7, namely a great-grandchild, he falls under “lineal descendants of the husband or wife,” which is a person entitled to file an action under the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 851. Moreover, whether the Plaintiff may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Independence Merit Treatment Act is not something to be strictly examined and determined ex officio, and once it is shown that the result of this case is likely to affect whether he may be registered as such a bereaved family member, he should be included among the persons entitled to sue as an interested person. Nevertheless, the lower court erred in its legal interpretation concerning standing as Plaintiff by failing to determine at all whether the Plaintiff, as a lineal descendant of Non-party 1, falls within the category of persons entitled to sue, and by holding that he lacked standing because he could not be registered as a bereaved family member under the former Independence Merit Treatment Act.
(2) However, the lower court, as an alternative determination, found that the evidence was insufficient to conclude that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 and between Non-party 7 and Non-party 2, and instead recognized that such natural parent-child relationships exist in light of the various circumstances. This falls within the exclusive province of the lower court as the trier of fact, and it does not appear to contain any error exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence. If so, even if this action is deemed lawful, the Plaintiff’s claim cannot be granted. Moreover, in this case, where only the Plaintiff appealed, setting aside the lower court judgment and dismissing the claim would result in a disadvantage to the Plaintiff; therefore, under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, the appeal has no choice but to be dismissed.
As stated above, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of the case, because the reasons differ, we state this in a separate opinion.

7. Supplementary opinion of Justice Park Jeong-hwa, Justice Kim Seon-su, and Justice Roh Jeong-hee regarding the majority opinion
We offer supplementary reasoning to the majority opinion on several points.

가. The majority opinion stated that among the “adult guardian, testamentary executor, or lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” listed in Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are cited in the provision at issue, only those who satisfy the requirements for filing suit under those provisions have standing as Plaintiff, and that standing as Plaintiff is not necessarily recognized where those requirements are not met. This is reasonable for the following reasons.
(1) The provision at issue does not directly regulate who the persons entitled to file such an action are. The provision at issue merely states that “a person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions” listed therein may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground. Accordingly, in light of the form, wording, and structure of the provision at issue, it is natural to interpret the persons who may file such an action as “persons who may file suit by satisfying the requirements under each provision” listed in the provision at issue.
(2) The requirements set forth in Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851 all pertain not to the grounds of an action for disavowal of paternity but to the “person entitled to sue.” Accordingly, the requirements concerning the “person entitled to sue” under those provisions should also apply to the persons entitled to file such an action.
(3) Since Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are cited in the provision at issue, are all supplementary provisions concerning the person entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity, the interpretive standard for determining “persons who may file such an action pursuant to those provisions” must be consistent. In other words, in the case of a testamentary executor under Civil Act Article 850, it should be interpreted that the executor may file an action for disavowal of paternity only when the husband or wife expresses by will an intent of denial, and that, pursuant to the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 850, the testamentary executor may file such an action only when the husband or wife has indicated by will an intent to deny the natural parent-child relationship. There is neither need nor reason to recognize standing as Plaintiff for a testamentary executor where there was no such will by the husband or wife.
(4) The separate opinion states that “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” under the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 851 may, without needing to satisfy the requirements set forth in those provisions, file such an action without restriction. Civil Act Article 851 does not automatically allow the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife to file an action for disavowal of paternity merely because the husband or wife has died; rather, it limits the filing period to cases where the husband dies before the child’s birth or where the husband or wife dies within the period for exercising the right of disavowal of paternity. This reflects the purpose of respecting the lifetime intent of the parties regarding the natural parent-child relationship and promoting stability in status order by permitting, exceptionally, persons other than the party entitled to disavow paternity(lineal ascendants or lineal descendants) to file an action for disavowal of paternity where the husband or wife had no opportunity during life even to file such an action or died before the period for exercising the right of disavowal expired and thus could not realize that intent.
However, if, as in the separate opinion, “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” may file such an action without any restriction under the provision at issue, the result may be to undermine the purpose of Civil Act Article 851, which exceptionally allows persons who are not entitled to disavow paternity to file an action for disavowal of paternity only in limited cases. As the majority opinion explains, a natural parent-child relationship can be formed diversely not only on the basis of blood relations but also on the basis of the parties’ intent, and the presumption of legitimacy may also apply to a parent-child relationship formed without a blood relationship. However, where the parties to such a parent-child relationship formed without blood relation(especially the parent) die and a considerable amount of time passes, it may become difficult to objectively determine whether the person recorded as a child in the family relations registration register is a person to whom the presumption of legitimacy applies. In such cases, “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife,” who originally could not file an action for disavowal of paternity due to the restrictions in Civil Act Article 851, may nonetheless contest the existence or nonexistence of the blood relationship against the intent of the parties by filing such an action. Furthermore, where a parent-child relationship formed without blood relation is substantially formed on the basis of the parties’ intent, as in cases where a child born through artificial insemination is registered as a biological child even though the presumption of legitimacy does not apply, or where a child born out of wedlock of a spouse is registered as a biological child while satisfying the requirements and intent to adopt(the Civil Act as amended in 2012 and effective as of 2013. 7. 1. requires approval from the Family Court when adopting a minor, but the supplementary provisions limit retroactive effect), legal protection should not be excluded merely because the presumption of legitimacy does not apply. Even where the parent did not raise any issue during his or her lifetime regarding the existence or nonexistence of blood relation with the child, allowing the parent’s lineal ascendants or other lineal descendants to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against the child on the ground that there was no blood relation after the parent’s death may infringe the personality rights or right to pursue happiness of the parties concerning the formation of family relations. Accordingly, the separate opinion’s view that such an action may be filed without restriction merely because one is a lineal ascendant or lineal descendant of the husband or wife is not appropriate.
(5) The majority opinion’s interpretation, which narrows as much as possible the scope of persons whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized under the provision at issue, is not unrelated to the fact that the provision at issue designates interested persons as persons entitled to file such an action. Even if standing as Plaintiff is not necessarily recognized under the provision at issue, such an action may still be filed where the person qualifies as an interested person; therefore, it is appropriate to interpret the scope of automatic persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue as above.

나. We now consider the standard for determining the scope of an interested person.
(1) The persons entitled to file such an action under the provision at issue include interested persons. Because an interested person is a broad concept meaning a third party with a legal interest in the existence or nonexistence of another person’s natural parent-child relationship, it is important in practice to determine its specific scope. The majority opinion limits interested persons to those whose rights, obligations, or legal status concerning inheritance, support, or the like are concretely affected by the final and conclusive judgment on the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. By contrast, the separate opinion states that in order to have standing as Plaintiff as an interested person, the person must have an interest worthy of legal protection to correct the record in the family relations registration register, and that this should be based on whether the person suffers detriment in legal status grounded in a status relationship due to a record in the family relations registration register contrary to the true blood relationship. However, the respective standards proposed by the majority opinion and the separate opinion do not in practice create a significant difference in determining whether a person is an interested person. This is because, even under the majority opinion, one examines what concrete effect exists on the person’s rights, obligations, or legal status concerning inheritance, support, or the like, and therefore, contrary to the concern expressed in the separate opinion, a third party who has no effect on status relationships and only a property interest will not be included among interested persons. In fact, it is difficult to find cases in prior Supreme Court precedents or lower court practice in which such a person was recognized as an interested person.
(2) The separate opinion points out that if whether a person qualifies as an interested person is to be determined individually in each case, there is a side effect whereby the focus of the family court’s examination and determination shifts from the subject matter of the litigation, namely the “existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship,” to the Plaintiff’s “rights, obligations, or impact on legal status,” or that the family court will bear the burden of having to interpret and determine administrative statutes.
However, since the provision at issue expressly designates interested persons as persons entitled to file such an action, where the Plaintiff asserts that he or she filed such an action as an interested person, a stage must be gone through to determine whether the Plaintiff actually qualifies as such. Such review of party capacity also has practical value in harmoniously realizing the two ideas governing parent-child relationships, namely securing the legal stability of parent-child relationships and the principle of blood truth. Moreover, the need to reasonably adjust the scope of party capacity and establish criteria for such determination before proceeding to the merits is not a problem unique to family litigation cases. Today, family litigation cases often raise legal issues from other areas, including public law relations, but this is an unavoidable result of the very diverse and complex manner in which legal interests surrounding status relationships are manifested. Accordingly, the side effects pointed out by the separate opinion are not matters that must essentially be considered in determining the scope of interested persons and the principles for examining and deciding that issue.

As stated above, we present this supplementary opinion regarding the majority opinion."}

1. Judgment on the grounds for appeal as to 피고 1
가. 아내가 혼인 중 artificial insemination으로 임신하여 출산한 자녀의 parent-child relationship
(1) 인공수정 자녀에 대한 presumption of paternity 규정 적용 여부
민법은 부모와 자녀의 친자관계 성립에 관하여 blood ties에 기초한 친생자관계(제844조 이하에서 natural child에 관한 규정을 두고 있다)와 당사자의 intent에 기초한 양자관계(제866조 이하에서 adoption에 관한 규정을 두고 있다)로 구분하고 있다. 이 중 친생자관계는 출생에 의하여 발생하는 부모와 자녀 관계로서, 부모가 natural sexual intercourse로 임신한 자녀를 출산한 경우를 전제로 하므로 부모와 출생한 자녀 사이에는 biological blood relationship이 존재하는 것이 원칙이다.
친생자관계에서도 mother-child relationship과 father-child relationship은 different하게 나타난다. 임신과 출산이라는 natural fact에 의하여 그 관계가 clearly 결정되는 mother-child relationship과 달리, father-child relationship은 그 관계 확정을 위한 별도의 requisites가 필요하다. 민법은 혼인 중에 아내가 임신한 자녀를 남편의 자녀로 추정하는 presumption of paternity 규정(제844조 제1항. 이하 ‘presumption of paternity 규정’이라 한다)을 두고 있다. 혼인외 출생자의 경우에는 biological father가 이를 인정하거나(제855조 제1항) 자녀가 부를 상대로 acknowledgement action(인지청구의 소, 제863조)을 제기하여 친생자관계의 존재를 확정하는 방법으로 법률상 친자관계를 창설할 수 있는데, 이때 부와 자녀 사이에 blood relationship이 존재하는지가 증명의 대상이 되는 principal fact를 구성한다(대법원 2002. 6. 14. 선고 2001므1537 판결, 대법원 2015. 6. 11. 선고 2014므8217 판결 등 참조).
피고 1에 대한 이 사건 청구의 issue는 아내가 혼인 중 남편이 아닌 제3자의 정자를 제공받아 natural means가 아닌 artificial insemination으로 임신한 자녀(이하 ‘artificial insemination child’라 한다)를 출산한 경우 출생한 자녀의 친자관계를 어떠한 standard로 인정해야 하는가이다(인공수정에는 다양한 forms가 있다. 여기에서는 위와 같은 ‘third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination’ 이외의 사안은 다루지 않는다). 현행 민법에는 인공수정 자녀의 친자관계 성립에 관해서 express provision이 없다. 1958. 2. 22. 민법 제정 당시에는 아내가 artificial insemination으로 자녀를 임신할 수 있다는 possibility를 상정하지 못하였기 때문에 이에 관한 규정을 둘 수 없었다.
그러나 친생자와 관련된 민법 규정, especially presumption of paternity 규정의 text and structure, 민법이 혼인 중 출생한 자녀의 legal status에 관하여 presumption of paternity 규정을 두고 있는 basic legislative purpose and history, 그리고 헌법이 보장하고 있는 marriage and family system 등에 비추어 보면, 아내가 혼인 중 남편이 아닌 제3자의 정자를 제공받아 artificial insemination으로 자녀를 출산한 경우에도 presumption of paternity 규정을 적용하여 artificial insemination으로 출생한 자녀가 남편의 자녀로 presumed된다고 보는 것이 타당하다. detailed reasons는 다음과 같다.
(가) 먼저 presumption of paternity 규정의 meaning에 관하여 본다.
모자관계는 출산이라는 사실에 의하여 친자관계가 성립하는 so-called natural parent-child relationship인 반면, 부자관계는 natural fact의 유무를 알 수 없어 법률이 인정하는 경우에만 친자관계가 성립한다는 의미에서 legal parent-child relationship이다. presumption of paternity 규정은 아내가 혼인 중에 임신한 자녀를 출산한 경우 그 자녀를 남편의 natural child로 추정하고 있다. 나아가 민법은 혼인 중의 임신 사실을 directly 증명하는 것이 쉽지 않다는 점을 고려하여 혼인이 성립한 날부터 200일 후 또는 혼인관계가 종료된 날부터 300일 이내에 출생한 자녀는 혼인 중에 임신한 것으로 추정하여(제844조 제2항, 제3항) uniform criteria에 따라 혼인 중 임신 여부를 정할 수 있도록 하였다. 이러한 presumption of paternity 규정은 parent-child relationship의 scientific verification이 practically impossible하고 법률상 혼인관계에 있는 아내가 남편의 자녀를 임신할 것이라는 사회적·법률적 background를 기초로 혼인 중 출생한 자녀가 남편과 blood relationship이 있을 probability가 높다는 것을 전제로 하고 있다.
presumption of paternity 규정은 그 자체로 true blood relationship과 일치하지 않는 legal parent-child relationship을 발생시킬 possibility를 내포하고 있다. 법률상 친자관계를 진실한 blood relationship에 부합시킬 수 있도록 하는 것이 헌법이 보장하고 있는 marriage and family system의 principle이라고 볼 수 있으므로(헌법재판소 1997. 3. 27. 선고 95헌가14, 96헌가7 전원재판부 결정 등 참조), 이를 위해 민법은 presumption of paternity 규정에 따라 형성된 father-child relationship을 제거할 수 있는 means로서 denial of paternity right를 남편과 아내에게 인정하고 있다(제847조. 이하 ‘action for disavowal of paternity 규정’이라 한다). 그러나 친생부인권을 행사할 수 있는 period를 너무 길게 인정하거나 그 period를 제한하지 않으면 자녀의 status를 promptly 확정해야 할 필요성과 status relations의 stability를 해칠 수 있으므로, 민법은 친생부인의 소는 남편 또는 아내가 cause for disavowal of paternity를 안 날부터 2년 내에 제기하여야 한다는 filing period를 정하고 있다(제847조 제1항). 이와 같이 standing과 filing period를 제한하는 action for disavowal of paternity 규정에 따라 presumption of paternity의 effect는 법률에서 인정하는 other presumptions보다 stronger force를 갖는다. 친생부인이 되지 않아 natural child로 추정되는 한 biological father가 혼인외 출생자로서 acknowledgement할 수도 없고 자녀가 biological father를 상대로 acknowledgement action을 제기할 수도 없으며, filing period가 지난 다음에는 그 presumption이 truth에 반하는 것으로 밝혀지더라도 overturn할 수 없다.
민법은 이와 같이 presumption of paternity 규정과 이에 대한 rebuttal method인 action for disavowal of paternity 규정을 strictly 정하고 있고, 친생부인을 할 수 없게 된 경우 자녀의 legal status가 finally 확정된다. 따라서 혼인 중 출생한 자녀의 father-child relationship은 민법 규정에 따라 uniformly 정해지는 것이고 그 blood relationship을 individually and concretely examine하여 정해지는 것이 아니다. 즉, 민법은 혼인관계에서 출생한 자녀라는 fact에 근거하여 normatively parent-child relationship이라는 family relationship을 형성하고 그와 같이 formed된 family relationship에 strong legal protection을 부여한다. 이처럼 general and institutional aspects에서 자녀의 welfare를 보호하면서도 presumption of paternity 규정에 따라 형성된 status relationship을 deny하고자 하는 사람에게는 reasonable methods and time을 정하여 status relationship에서 벗어날 수 있도록 함으로써 친자관계 확정을 둘러싸고 conflicting interests를 coordinate하는 것이 민법의 basic attitude이다.
혼인 중 출생한 자녀에 대한 presumption of paternity의 standard를 어떻게 정할 것인가의 issue는 부부와 자녀의 legal status와 related된 것으로서 ‘법률적인 친자관계를 진실에 합치시키고자 하는 부부·자녀의 interest’와 ‘친자관계의 prompt determination을 통하여 legal stability를 찾고자 하는 자녀의 interest’를 social reality나 traditional conception에 맞게 how to harmonize할 것인가에 관한 issue이다. 이는 interested parties의 basic rights, marriage and family life에 관한 constitutional decision을 고려하여 결정할 issue로서 in principle legislature’s discretion에 맡겨져 있다(헌법재판소 2015. 4. 30. 선고 2013헌마623 전원재판부 결정 참조). 민법은 presumption of paternity 규정과 action for disavowal of paternity 규정을 통하여 혼인 중 임신하여 출생한 자녀에 대한 parent-child relationship setting standard에 관한 legislative decision을 하였다고 볼 수 있다.
(나) presumption of paternity 규정을 artificial insemination child에도 equally 적용해야 하는 reason에 관하여 본다.
legal interpretation의 goal은 legal stability를 침해하지 않는 범위에서 concrete appropriateness를 pursue하는 데 있다. 이를 위하여 가능한 한 법률에 사용된 문언의 ordinary meaning에 faithful하게 법률을 interpret하는 것이 principle이지만, 문언의 ordinary meaning을 벗어나지 않는 범위에서는 법률의 legislative purpose and object, enactment and amendment history, harmony with the legal order as a whole, other statutes and regulations과의 relation 등을 고려하는 systematic and logical interpretation method를 additional하게 동원하여 법해석의 goal에 맞는 reasonable interpretation을 할 수 있다(대법원 2009. 4. 23. 선고 2006다81035 판결, 대법원 2014. 12. 11. 선고 2013므4591 판결, 대법원 2016. 11. 25. 선고 2015두37815 판결 등 참조). 그리고 enactment 당시 예정하지 않은 phenomenon도 legislative solution이 없으면 current legal system의 structure에 incorporated시켜 more reasonable solution을 도모하여야 한다.
presumption of paternity 규정은 아내가 혼인 중에 임신한 자녀를 남편의 자녀로 추정한다고 정하고 있을 뿐이다. text상 이 규정은 임신하게 된 specific circumstances에 따라 presumption의 application을 제한하거나 natural means가 아닌 artificial insemination으로 임신한 자녀에 대해서 presumption의 application을 exclude하지 않는다. 이러한 form은 2017. 10. 31. 법률 제14965호로 개정될 때에도 그대로 유지되었다. 그 밖에 민법의 다른 규정을 보더라도 artificial insemination child에 대하여 presumption of paternity 규정의 application을 exclude하거나 제한하지 않는다. 따라서 artificial insemination child에 presumption of paternity 규정을 적용하는 것은 법률 문언이 허용하는 interpretation의 범위 내에 있다.
헌법 제36조 제1항은 “혼인과 family life는 개인의 dignity와 양성의 equality를 기초로 성립되고 유지되어야 하며, 국가는 이를 guarantee한다.”라고 정하여 individual autonomous will과 gender equality에 기초한 marriage와 이를 바탕으로 formed되는 family life를 protect하고 있다. presumption of paternity 규정은 이러한 constitutional principle을 바탕으로 부부가 정상적인 혼인생활을 하고 있는 경우 이를 기초로 formed되는 family relationship에 stable legal status를 부여하여 household peace를 유지하는 데에 기여한다. artificial insemination child가 birth하게 된 background가 된 marital relationship, 그리고 혼인 중 artificial insemination child가 birth함에 따라 발생하게 되는 parent-child relationship 등의 family relationship도 이처럼 respected되어야 할 individual and family autonomy에 기초하여 formed된 것이므로 혼인 중 출생한 other children과 discriminate해서는 안 된다. marriage를 바탕으로 formed된 family life에 대한 protection의 necessity는 혼인 중 출생한 자녀가 artificial insemination child라는 reason으로 달라지지 않는다. 임신하게 된 specific circumstances에 따라 혼인 중 출생한 자녀의 legal status가 달라진다고 볼 legal basis가 없다. normal marital relationship을 유지하고 있는 상태에서 birth한 artificial insemination child에 대해서 sexual intercourse에 의해 출생한 자가 아니라는 reason으로 presumption of paternity 규정의 application을 exclude할 rational reason도 없다.
presumption of paternity 규정은 혼인 중 출생한 자녀에 대해서 출생과 동시에 stable legal status를 부여하여 legal protection의 vacuum을 없애고자 한 것이다. 이것은 혼인 중 artificial insemination으로 출생한 자녀에 대해서도 same하다.
sexual intercourse나 biological blood relationship만을 parent-child relationship formation의 basis로 삼거나 이를 reason으로 artificial insemination child가 남편의 자녀로 추정될 수 없다고 보는 것은 혼인 중 출생한 artificial insemination child에 대해서 father를 정할 수 없는 state를 초래한다. 이는 artificial insemination child의 legal status를 불안하게 함으로써 민법이 presumption of paternity 규정을 두게 된 system purpose와 directly opposite되어 unfair하다. artificial insemination child에 대해서 presumption of paternity 규정을 적용하지 않고 biological blood relationship만을 priority할 경우에는 더욱 unfair한 result를 초래한다. 정자를 제공한 third party가 anonymous인 경우에는 donor를 specific하기 어렵다. donor는 자신의 정자로 태어날 child에 대해서 father로서 책임져야 한다는 것을 예상할 수 없어 father role을 기대하기 어려울 뿐만 아니라, anonymously sperm을 제공한 것 외에 자녀의 임신과 출생에 대해서 father as status를 귀속시킬 만한 다른 role을 하지 않는다. 따라서 blood relationship이 있다는 point만으로 donor를 immediately legal father로 취급하거나 그에게 legal father로서의 responsibility를 묻는 것은 타당하지 않다. 이처럼 artificial insemination child에 대해서 presumption of paternity 규정에 따라 father-child relationship을 정하지 않으면 사실상 father-child relationship을 정할 수 없게 되거나 민법이 예상하지 않은 father-child relationship을 성립하도록 하는 등 unfair한 results를 가져온다.
요컨대, presumption of paternity 규정은 혼인 중 출생한 자녀에 대해서 적용되는데, 그 text와 legislative purpose, marriage and family life에 대한 constitutional guarantee 등에 비추어 혼인 중 출생한 artificial insemination child도 혼인 중 출생한 자녀에 포함된다고 보아야 한다.
(다) child welfare는 친자관계의 성립과 유지에서 most important factor이므로, artificial insemination child에 대해서 presumption of paternity 규정이 적용되는지를 따질 때에도 child welfare에 focus를 두어야 한다. child welfare는 단순히 child에게 protection and upbringing이라는 parent-child relationship의 substance를 제공하는 것에 limited되지 않고 이에 corresponding하는 legal parent-child relationship을 형성해 줌으로써 parents가 역할을 할 수 있도록 해야 하고, 이에 따라 parents가 child development를 위한 support를 충분히 할 수 있도록 institutionally guarantee해 주어야 한다. child welfare를 지속적으로 책임지는 parent에게 child와의 status relationship을 귀속시키는 것이 child welfare에 도움이 된다. artificial insemination child에 대해서 natural parent-child relationship이 생기지 않는다고 보는 것은 artificial insemination child를 양육해 왔던 married couple에게 huge shock일 뿐만 아니라 이를 바탕으로 family relationship을 formed해 온 child에게도 irreparable risk라고 할 수 있다.
(라) artificial insemination child의 birth process와 이를 둘러싼 family relationship의 actual form에 비추어 보더라도 artificial insemination child에 대해서 presumption of paternity 규정을 적용하는 것에 social appropriateness를 인정할 수 있다.
artificial insemination의 경우 natural sexual intercourse라는 element가 없는 대신 artificial insemination 또는 embryo transfer라는 auxiliary act가 존재한다. 아내가 third party sperm을 통한 artificial insemination 방법으로 자녀를 임신하는 데에 남편이 동의하는 경우 부부는 artificial insemination child가 남편과 blood relationship이 없더라도 child에 대해서 jointly 책임진다고 예상하였을 것이고 그 동의에 따라 born한 child와 parent-child relationship을 형성하게 된다고 보아야 한다. 남편은 아내가 artificial insemination으로 인한 임신과 출산을 하는 과정에 동의함으로써 participation하게 되고 그 과정에서 출생한 자녀는 부부 사이의 natural sexual intercourse로 임신·출산한 자녀와 마찬가지로 부부 사이에 혼인 중 출생한 자녀라고 볼 수 있다. 이러한 parent-child relationship을 바탕으로 artificial insemination child는 부부 사이의 자녀로서 그들과 substantive parent-child relationship의 모습을 formed하고 유지한다. 사회적으로도 이와 같이 formed된 parent-child relationship은 natural sexual intercourse로 출생한 자녀의 경우와 마찬가지로 부부의 child로 accepted되고 있다.
그런데도 presumption of paternity 규정의 application을 exclude하거나 artificial insemination child에 대해서 부부와 legal parent-child relationship이 성립되지 않는다고 한다면, 이는 legal stability와 peace를 깨뜨려 artificial insemination child를 legal protection이 없는 vacuum state로 만드는 것으로서 우리 사회에서 받아들이기 어렵다.
(2) 인공수정 자녀에 대한 disavowal of paternity 허용 여부
(가) 위에서 보았듯이 action for disavowal of paternity 규정은 legal parent-child relationships를 truth에 부합시키고자 하는 interest를 위하여 마련되었다. 그러나 blood relationship이 없는 child가 출생하였다는 점이 밝혀진 경우에는 presumption of paternity 규정 application의 premise가 없어진 것으로 볼 수 있다. 이러한 경우 민법은 남편과 아내가 household life와 status relations에서 누려야 할 personality rights, right to pursue happiness, 그리고 개인의 dignity와 gender equality에 기초한 marriage and family life에 관한 fundamental rights를 보장하기 위하여 이들에게 reasonable period within scope에서 친생부인의 소를 제기할 수 있도록 하고 있다(헌법재판소 1997. 3. 27. 선고 95헌가14, 96헌가7 전원재판부 결정 등 참조).
presumption of paternity 규정에 따라 artificial insemination child를 남편의 자녀로 추정하는 reason은 ‘consent’를 함으로써 임신·출산 과정에 participation한 부부 사이에 출생한 자녀에 대해서 presumption of paternity 규정을 적용하는 것이 헌법과 민법을 비롯한 전체 family law system에 비추어 justified되기 때문이다. artificial insemination child에 대해서 presumption of paternity 규정을 적용하는 것은 혼인관계에 있는 부부의 household life와 status relationship을 guarantee해 주면서 free will에 따라 family relationships을 formed하고 socially recognized family relationship의 substance를 legally secure하기 위한 것이다.
artificial insemination child를 임신하여 출산하는 과정에 비추어 볼 때, artificial insemination child가 남편과 아내의 sexual intercourse로 임신한 것이 아니고 이에 따라 child가 남편과 blood relationship이 없다는 점은 모두 artificial insemination child에 대해서 presumption of paternity 규정을 적용할 때에 already 고려한 사항들로서, artificial insemination child가 출생할 당시 남편이 알고 있던 fact와 다르지 않다. 이러한 premise facts를 바탕으로 presumption of paternity 규정을 통하여 artificial insemination child를 남편의 자녀로 presumed하는 것은 남편이 household life와 status relations에서 누려야 할 personality rights, right to pursue happiness, 그리고 개인의 dignity와 gender equality에 기초한 marriage and family life에 관한 fundamental rights를 guarantee하고 이를 realize해 주기 위한 것이다. 이와 반대로 남편에게 친생부인의 소를 제기할 수 있도록 하는 것이 남편의 fundamental right라고 말할 수 없다.
action for disavowal of paternity는 natural sexual intercourse로 임신·출산한 자녀에 대해서 sexual intercourse process가 없다는 것과 이에 따라 biological blood relationship이 없다는 것을 requirement로 제기할 수 있다. artificial insemination child에 대해서도 위와 같은 requirement로 action for disavowal of paternity를 제기할 수 있다고 한다면 친생자관계는 biological blood으로 결정된다는 것을 전제로 하는 것으로서 artificial insemination을 통한 친자관계의 형성을 deny하는 result가 된다. 이는 민법이 presumption of paternity 규정과 action for disavowal of paternity 규정을 두어 혈연 이외의 other elements도 고려하여 친생자관계를 정하고자 한 purpose와 목적에 accord하지 않는다.
(나) normally marital life를 하고 있는 부부 사이에서 artificial insemination child가 출생하는 경우 남편은 consent의 방법으로 child의 임신과 출산에 participation하게 되는데, 이것이 presumption of paternity 규정이 적용되는 basis라고 할 수 있다. 남편이 artificial insemination에 동의하였다가 나중에 이를 reverse하고 action for disavowal of paternity를 제기하는 것은 허용되지 않는다. 나아가 artificial insemination consent와 관련된 current legal system의 deficiencies, artificial insemination이 이루어지는 medical reality, 민법 제852조에서 친생자임을 승인한 자의 친생부인을 제한하고 있는 purpose 등에 비추어 이러한 consent가 명백히 밝혀지지 않았던 circumstances가 있다고 해서 곧바로 parent-child relationship이 denied된다거나 action for disavowal of paternity를 제기할 수 있다고 볼 것은 아니다.
